blocks.text: So far every review you can read is a happy one. But roughly half of this corpus is complaints — and complaints all run on one grammatical engine: negation. This lesson gives you the words for what goes wrong (vika, ongelma, rikki), and the actual mechanics of how Finnish says 'not', which you've already glimpsed with en suosittele in Lesson 1.

blocks.title: Finnish complaints don't soften
blocks.text: Where an English review might say 'unfortunately this didn't quite work out', Finnish reviewers state the failure flatly: vika ei korjaantunut, full stop. There's no cushioning phrase before it. This bluntness isn't rudeness by Finnish standards — it's just precision. Once you stop expecting a softening word, these reviews get much easier to read.
Piece 1 — Naming what's wrong: vika, ongelma, rikki

blocks.content: {Vika|word|noun|fault/defect} is a fault or defect — something specifically broken about a part or diagnosis. {Ongelma|word|noun|problem} is the general word for 'problem', wider than vika. {Rikki|word|adjective|broken} isn't a noun at all — it's a predicate word that pairs with on/oli, just like hyvä did in Lesson 1: auto on rikki, 'the car is broken'.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Negation: swapping en for ei

blocks.title: The negation verb changes with the subject
blocks.text: From Lesson 1 you know en suosittele — 'I don't recommend'. En is the 'I' form of Finnish negation. When the subject is 'it' (like auto, vika, ongelma), the word changes to {ei|grammar|negation, 3rd person|does not/did not}. Same job, different person: en (I don't), ei (it doesn't). The main verb itself drops its ending either way — this bare form is called the connegative.

blocks.content: Here's the twist: in the past tense, ei is followed not by a plain verb stem but by a past participle ending in {-nut|grammar|past participle suffix|-ed (past participle)} or -nyt. Toimia (to work/function) becomes toiminut. So 'it didn't work' is ei toiminut — not ei toimi-past. This is a genuinely new pattern, so let's see it a few times.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: Don't panic at the word 'participle'. You already know the shape from English: 'broken', 'fixed', 'solved' are all participles too. Finnish just always uses this same -nut/-nyt shape after ei in the past, no matter the verb. Spot the -nut/-nyt ending and you'll recognise this pattern instantly, everywhere.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Did the car work after the service?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Ei, auto ei toiminut. Vika ei korjaantunut.
lines.en: No, the car didn't work. The fault wasn't fixed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kyllä, ja ongelma jatkui. En suosittele tätä korjaamoa.
lines.en: Yes, and the problem continued. I don't recommend this repair shop.

blocks.title: Free word from the dialogue
blocks.text: Edelleen means 'still' — a very useful word for complaints: auto on edelleen rikki, 'the car is still broken'. Jatkui comes from jatkua, 'to continue' — ongelma jatkui, 'the problem continued'.

blocks.content: Vika: VI-ka (short, sharp, stress on VI). Ongelma: ON-gel-ma (three even syllables — the 'g' is soft, close to English 'g' in 'go'). Korjaantunut: KOR-yaan-tu-nut (long word — break it into KOR-yaan, then tu-nut, and it stops feeling intimidating).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: vika, ongelma, rikki — fault, problem, broken
en / ei / eivät — negation changes with the subject: I / it / they don't
the past-negative pattern: ei + past participle (ei toiminut, ei auttanut, ei korjaantunut)
You can now read and write a full negative review, not just a positive one
You recognise the -nut/-nyt ending as 'past participle' wherever it appears
